And, as embodied by Michael Urie in the happy revival of Harvey Fierstein’s “Torch Song,” which opened on Thursday night, Arnold is just the guy and gal to pull you out of your election-season weariness.
Kaufman and his cast hit every note of humor and heartache in a durable work.
Harvey Fierstein is back on Broadway and better than ever in 'Torch Song'
Urie triumphs in this play, primarily through the brilliance of his physical comedy.
Fierstein's performance is a master class in controlled emotion, balancing camp theatricality with genuine pathos in a way that feels both nostalgic and immediate.
This safe production suggests but never fully summons the ache behind the wisecracks, or the dangers and the loneliness gay people had to endure in the 1970s, when the story is largely set.
The play's defiant and universal humanity shines through with a burning intensity in Moises Kaufman's beautifully modulated production.
On stage, most of the two and a half plus hours, he takes us laughing and crying on an emotional journey that will leave you ragged and raw.
In the story of Arnold, Torch Song supplies one of theatre’s truest, most holistic and funny distillations of what gay pride really means: its cost, its benefits, and its necessity.
That’s when Torch Song really seems to catch fire.
The histrionics may be effective, but they go some distance towards cheapening the tone
While “Torch Song” lacks the brilliance of “Angels in America” and the bite of “The Boys in the Band,” it is well worth a second look.
Every character has plenty of opportunity to emote and vent, and the narrative flows smoothly.
The creeping feeling that Torch Song is more dated than we’d hoped takes hold and won’t let go.
As it is, Torch Song feels like a curious antique gathering dust.

Mr. Fierstein knew that wasn’t true 40 years ago, and fortunately for today’s theatergoers, he was brave enough to write about it.
And Urie alone is worth the price of admission.
The piece still works, it feels fresh and revolutionary all over again.
It transcends merely being a history play and remains instead a lively and funny show that features a new high from the always-likeable Urie.
An uproarious comedy with a suite of characters you come to love, “Torch Song” is a must-see of the fall (or any) season.
Torch Song still holds up more than 36 years later as an epic of LGBTQ life that has a lot to say about sexuality, family, gender roles, love and acceptance to a new generation.
Urie works harder than you can imagine: cracking jokes with razor-sharp timing, imbuing certain throw-away moments with peerless physical abandon, and, above all, piercing the heart time and again.
